Within-person effects

Source: vignettes/within-person.Rmd
within-person.Rmd

With panel data, the effect of a variable that changes over time can come from differences between people (people who are married compared with people who are not) or from changes within a person (the same person when married compared with when not married). A random-effects model mixes the two. The correlated random effects (Mundlak) specification isolates the within-person effect: add each time-varying predictor’s person mean to a random-effects model, and the marginal effect of the predictor, holding its person mean fixed, is then the within-person effect.

The data are those of the panel models example: depressive symptoms among adults aged 51 and older in a 30% sample of households from the Health and Retirement Study, 2010 to 2020. Marital status and age change over time, so each gets its person mean.

library(suest)
library(marginaleffects)
library(haven)
library(lme4)

hrs <- zap_labels(read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/hrs_si_2025.dta"))
hrs <- subset(hrs, year >= 2010 & age >= 51 & (hhidpn %/% 1000) %% 10 < 3)
hrs$depressed <- as.numeric(hrs$cesd >= 4)
vars <- c("depressed", "marstatB", "age", "woman", "race4cat", "collegeB")
hrs <- hrs[complete.cases(hrs[vars]), ]
hrs$mean_marstatB <- ave(hrs$marstatB, hrs$hhidpn)
hrs$mean_age <- ave(hrs$age, hrs$hhidpn)
hrs[c("marstatB", "woman", "race4cat", "collegeB")] <-
  lapply(hrs[c("marstatB", "woman", "race4cat", "collegeB")], factor)

re <- glmer(depressed ~ marstatB + I(age - 65) + woman + race4cat + collegeB +
              (1 | hhidpn), family = binomial, data = hrs, nAGQ = 25,
            control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
cre <- glmer(depressed ~ marstatB + mean_marstatB + I(age - 65) + I(mean_age - 65) +
               woman + race4cat + collegeB + (1 | hhidpn), family = binomial,
             data = hrs, nAGQ = 25, control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
fit <- suest(re, cre, model_names = c("Random effects", "Within-person"))

The marginal effect of being married in each model, and the difference:

married <- avg_comparisons(fit, variables = "marstatB", newdata = hrs)
married
#> 
#>           Group Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)     S   2.5 %  97.5 %
#>  Random effects  -0.0958    0.00617 -15.5   <0.001 178.1 -0.1079 -0.0837
#>  Within-person   -0.0656    0.01113  -5.9   <0.001  28.0 -0.0874 -0.0438
#> 
#> Term: marstatB
#> Type: response
#> Comparison: 1 - 0
hypotheses(married, hypothesis = difference ~ revpairwise)
#> 
#>                          Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)    S   2.5 %  97.5 %
#>  (Random effects) - (Within-person)  -0.0302    0.00867 -3.48   <0.001 11.0 -0.0472 -0.0132

Example interpretation: In the random-effects model, being married is associated with a 9.6 percentage point reduction in the probability of depressive symptoms. Examining only within-person variation, the effect of being married is a 6.6 percentage point reduction. The random-effects estimate is 3.0 points larger (p<.001p < .001) because it pools both between- and within-person variation.
